title: Arrays
learningGoals: make an array with a starting list
read and change items by index

youtube.title: C++ Arrays: Store Many Values in One Variable | C++ Programming EP 31
youtube.description: In this episode you will make an array with a starting list, read and change items by index and stay inside the array size, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Arrays · 1:23 Five marks · 2:33 Boxes side by side · 3:24 Second program · 4:50 Recap · 5:23 Bug of the Day · 6:20 Challenge · 6:44 Next episode

thumbnail.visual: big text "ARRAYS" in tomato on butter; Xecxec next to a row of five numbered lockers; thin black border and drop shadow.
thumbnail.pose: Xecxec next to a row of five numbered lockers

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we store many values under one name. An array is a row of boxes, side by side in memory.

scenes.onScreen: "Arrays": numbered lines (1. An array holds many values of one type; 2. The size is fixed; 3. Indexes start at zero) and an analogy card: a row of lockers: one name on the row, one number on each door
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: An array holds many values of the same type. You choose the size when you make it, and the size never changes. Each item has an index. The first index is zero. The items sit side by side in memory. Think of a row of lockers. The row has one name, and each door has its own number. Why use an array? Imagine five marks in five separate variables. You would write five names, and a loop could not reach them. With an array, one name holds all five, and a loop can visit each one. Arrays are everywhere. A list of prices, the pixels of a photo and the scores of a game all live in arrays.
points: An array holds many values of one type

analogy.title: Arrays
analogy.body: A row of lockers: one name on the row, one number on each door

scenes.onScreen: marks.cpp: an array of five marks, read by index
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 5] The number in square brackets is the size. The list in braces gives the starting values. [HL 6] Index zero is the first item. It prints seventy-two. [HL 7] Index four is the last item. It prints fifty-eight. There is no index five. [HL 8] We can change one item by its index. [HL 9] Now the third item prints seventy. [HL 5] Read the line in parts. The type is int, and the name is marks. The number five in square brackets is the size. The curly braces hold the starting values, in order. [HL 6] The first item has index zero, so marks of zero is seventy-two. [HL 7] The last item has index four, one less than the size. [HL 8] You can change an item with an equals sign, like a plain variable.

scenes.onScreen: five int boxes in a row, each with an address four bytes after the last
scenes.animation: Boxes pop in one by one with size and address tags; arrows draw on as the narrator mentions them; regions are labelled; pop per box
scenes.narration: Look at the memory. Each box holds one mark. Each box is four bytes wide. So the addresses grow by four each time. The computer finds any item by a simple sum. It takes the start address and adds the index times four. Notice that the items sit side by side. Each int takes four bytes, so each address is four more than the one before. That is why the computer finds any item at once. It starts at the first address and adds the index times four.

scenes.onScreen: sumall.cpp: a loop adds all five marks
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 6] The sum starts at zero. [HL 7] The loop runs with i from zero up to four. The test says less than five, so five is never used. [HL 8] Each round adds one item to the sum. [TRACK sum=72] After round one the sum is seventy-two. [HL 10] At the end, the sum is three hundred and sixty-nine. [HL 6] The sum starts at zero before the loop. [HL 7] The loop counts from zero up to four. The test says less than five, so the index five is never used. [HL 8] Each round adds one mark to the sum. This is the standard way to walk through an array.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as sumall dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints Sum colon three hundred sixty-nine. Check the sum by hand. Seventy-two plus eighty-five is one hundred fifty-seven. Add sixty-four, ninety and fifty-eight to reach three hundred sixty-nine.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. An array holds many values of one type. Two. The size is fixed when you make the array. Three. Indexes start at zero, and the last index is size minus one. Four. The items sit side by side in memory. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: An array holds many values of one type.
The size is fixed when you make the array.
Indexes start at zero, and the last index is size minus one.
The items sit side by side in memory.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: Too many starting values
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the g++ error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. The array has three boxes, but the list has four values. The compiler says too many initializers. The fourth value has no box to go in. Make the size four, or remove one value. The size of an array is fixed, and the compiler counts your starting values. If you give more values than boxes, the compiler stops. If you give fewer, the rest become zero. You can also leave out the size, and the compiler counts for you.

scenes.onScreen: I asked my array how it feels. It said, I am fine, but I count from zero.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: I asked my array how it feels. It said, I am fine, but I count from zero.

scenes.onScreen: Task card: store and print five numbers
scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Make an array of five temperatures. Print the first one and the last one. Hint: the last index is the size minus one, so use index four for five items. Write your answer in the comments.

scenes.animation: Next-episode card slides up with a whoosh; right side stays empty for end-screen elements; sign-off text types in
scenes.narration: Next time: looping over arrays. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.error:
Compiler output (exactly as g++ prints it):

marks.cpp: In function 'int main()':
marks.cpp:5:35: error: too many initializers for 'int [3]'
    5 |     int marks[3] = {72, 85, 64, 90};
      |                                   ^
bug.why: The size says three boxes, but the list has four values. The compiler stops, because the fourth value has no box.

challengeAnswer: Write int temps with five values in braces. Print temps at index zero and temps at index four.
